test_title: PYST 56: RRB Group D - GS (Held On: 22 Dec, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: What is the role of sulphuric acid in the anodising process of aluminium?

options.text: It acts as an electrolyte to help form a thicker oxide layer.
It reacts with aluminium to form aluminium chloride.

solution:
The correct answer is __**It acts as an electrolyte to help form a thicker oxide layer**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Anodising** is an **electrochemical process** that converts the metal surface into a decorative, durable, and corrosion-resistant **anodic oxide finish**.
 
• In this process, **Sulphuric Acid** (usually at a **concentration of 15% to 20%**) serves as the **electrolyte**. An electrolyte is a medium that contains ions and conducts electricity through the movement of those ions.
 
• During the reaction, the **aluminium** object is made the **anode** (the positive electrode) in an electrolytic cell containing the acid. When an **electric current** is passed through the solution, water molecules are decomposed.
 
• Oxygen is released at the **anode** and reacts with the aluminium surface to form a controlled, uniform, and much **thicker layer of aluminium oxide (Al2O3)** than would occur naturally. ***Hence, the statement that it acts as an electrolyte to help form a thicker oxide layer is correct.***
 
• While **Sulphuric Acid** does have the potential to dissolve aluminium, in the context of **anodising**, its primary role is to facilitate the **oxidation** process by allowing current to flow and creating micro-pores that help the oxide layer grow deeper into the metal.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structure of the Oxide Layer:** The layer formed during **Sulphuric Acid anodising** (often called **Type II Anodizing**) is porous. These **microscopic pores** are essential because they allow the electrolyte to reach the unoxidized aluminium beneath, enabling the layer to continue growing to a thickness of **5 to 25 microns** or more.
 
• **Corrosion Resistance and Durability:** The resulting **aluminium oxide** layer is extremely hard (second only to diamond in some forms) and provides excellent **wear resistance** and protection against **atmospheric corrosion**.
 
• **Coloring and Aesthetics:** Because the anodic coating is **porous** before it is sealed, it can easily absorb **dyes** or pigments. This is how various colored aluminium products, such as electronics, cookware, and architectural panels, are produced.
 
• **Sealing Process:** After the oxide layer reaches the desired thickness, the part is usually "sealed" by immersion in **hot water** or chemical solutions. This converts the oxide into a **hydrated form**, closing the pores and locking in any dyes while increasing **corrosion resistance**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Comparison with Natural Oxidation:** Aluminium naturally forms a very thin, **passive oxide film** (about **2 to 3 nanometers** thick) when exposed to air. **Anodising** artificially increases this thickness by thousands of times to provide industrial-grade protection.
 
• **Other Types of Anodising:**
 
 
• **Type I:** Uses **Chromic Acid**, typically for aerospace parts where a thinner but highly corrosion-resistant layer is needed.
 
• **Type III:** Also known as **Hard Anodizing**, it uses **Sulphuric Acid** at lower temperatures and higher voltages to produce a very thick (up to **50-100 microns**) and wear-resistant coating.
 
 
 
• **Temperature Control:** During the process, the temperature of the **Sulphuric Acid** bath is usually maintained around **20°C (68°F)**. If the temperature rises too high, the acid begins to dissolve the oxide layer faster than it forms, resulting in a powdery or "burnt" finish.
 
• **Environmental Safety:** **Sulphuric Acid** is preferred over **Chromic Acid** in many modern applications because it is generally less toxic and easier to dispose of in compliance with **environmental regulations**.
